steps.answer:
I recomputed the figures and found an error in my earlier answer. For 3 frogs, the uniform baseline is 50%, not the 33% I wrote. With 3 frogs, k has only two candidates besides j, so chance is 1/2. The ratios of 1.8 and 1.4 are now confirmed by the tool output.

**Corrected answer:** Yes. Frogs return to the frog that called two calls earlier more often than chance predicts. This held in 29 of 32 recordings.

| | Share of sequences where k = i |
|---|---|
| Observed | 42.0% (5,424 of 12,910) |
| Uniform null (k equally likely among the frogs other than j) | 23.0% |
| Call-share null (k drawn by each frog's own call share, excluding j) | 30.1% |

- Observed returns are 1.82 times the uniform expectation and 1.39 times the call-share expectation.
- The paired Wilcoxon test on per-recording proportions gave p ≈ 3×10⁻⁸. The sequences overlap and are not independent, so treat that p-value as optimistic.

**By group size** (observed, uniform null, call-share null):

| Frogs | Observed | Uniform | Call-share |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 70.1% | 50.0% | 66.1% |
| 4 | 47.7% | 33.3% | 43.0% |
| 5 | 45.6% | 25.0% | 32.3% |
| 6 | 43.7% | 20.0% | 27.5% |
| 7 | 37.6% | 16.7% | 21.6% |
| 8 | 24.2% | 14.3% | 18.8% |

The excess is real at every group size. It is small for 3 frogs once call share is accounted for.

**Caveats**
- The data can't separate a true "answer the frog before last" tendency from simple alternation between two dominant callers.
- The call-share null is inflated by any back-and-forth pattern, so it is conservative.
- Some group sizes come from few recordings: 3 frogs from 1 recording and 8 frogs from 3.
- I didn't test for a difference between the 2023 and 2025 sessions.
